captions: July twenty-first, twenty twenty-six — Tuesday.
The market has closed for the day.
For the second day running, the Nifty and Sensex fell.
So what moved them today?
We'll break down the closing numbers, the stocks that fell,
and the sectors that rose.
This is information analysis only — not investment advice.
First, the closing numbers.
The Sensex fell two hundred thirty-eight points to close at 77,470 —
down about a third of a percent.
The Nifty 50 lost fifty-one points to settle at 24,188.
This was its second straight losing session.
But here's the crucial point —
the Midcap index rose a third of a percent,
and the Smallcap index gained more than half a percent.
That means most stocks were actually in the green.
This fall was limited to a handful of large stocks —
it was not a broad sell-off.
So why did it fall?
Four reasons.
The most important — crude oil and Middle East tension.
Yemen's Houthis threatened a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.
That raised fears over oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz,
pushing Brent crude to between eighty-eight and ninety dollars.
Since India imports most of its oil,
this pressures inflation and the rupee.
Second — weakness in IT stocks.
TCS and Infosys each fell about one percent.
Third — PSU banks, HDFC Bank, and SBI.
These high-weightage stocks dragged the Nifty down.
Fourth — foreign institutions stayed net sellers,
amid a risk-off mood across global markets.
Now the biggest losers today, and the reasons behind them.
First — Cipla.
The worst Nifty performer, down about two percent.
Pharma and healthcare stocks were weak across the board today.
Second — Doctor Reddy's and Max Healthcare,
both down more than one percent.
Third — TCS and Infosys.
These IT giants each fell about one percent,
on weak global tech sentiment and rupee moves.
Fourth — HDFC Bank and SBI.
Because these carry the highest weightage in the index,
even a small fall pulled the Nifty down noticeably.
Let's look at today's sector scoreboard — who fell,
and who rose?
On the losing side — Nifty PSU Bank fell the most,
followed by Nifty IT under pressure from TCS and Infosys.
FMCG stocks also saw selling in the afternoon.
On the winning side — the Nifty Chemical index rose the most,
followed by Cement.
When there's uncertainty,
investors rotate into these defensive sectors.
So while IT and banks fell, chemicals, cement,
and midcaps rose.
This is sector rotation — not a collapse of the whole market.
Here's the most important lesson from today —
why does crude oil move the market?
Many people think crude prices don't affect them.
But India imports about eighty-five percent of its oil.
When crude rises, the import bill, inflation,
and pressure on the rupee all go up.
But crude doesn't drag every stock equally.
For paints, airlines, and auto companies it's bad news —
crude is their raw material.
But for oil producers like ONGC, it's actually good news.
And one more key point — this isn't India's own problem.
A global geopolitical event —
the Houthis and the Strait of Hormuz — moved our market.
Markets are always connected to the world.
Five lessons from today.
One — even on a second down day, most stocks rose.
This was a narrow, large-cap-led fall.
Two —
crude near ninety dollars raises inflation and rupee pressure.
Keep an eye on it.
Three — while IT and banks fell, chemicals and cement rose.
This is sector rotation —
money moving from one sector to another.
Four —
global news like the Houthis and Hormuz directly moves our market.
Watch the world, not just India.
Five — for regular SIP investors,
one red day like this is just noise, not a long-term trend.
Don't panic-sell.
July twenty-first, at a glance.
The Sensex fell two hundred thirty-eight points and the Nifty fifty-one —
the second day down.
The cause —
crude crossing ninety dollars on Houthi and Hormuz fears,
weakness in IT and PSU banks, and foreign investor selling.
Cipla, Doctor Reddy's, TCS, Infosys, HDFC Bank, and SBI fell.
Chemicals, cement, midcaps, and smallcaps rose.
But breadth was positive — this was a narrow large-cap shock,
not a market crash.
One red day isn't the whole story —
long-term discipline is what really wins.

Thanks for watching.
